reference.source: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle
clinicalPearls: Pes planus is loss of the medial longitudinal arch, usually with hindfoot valgus and forefoot abduction, and may be physiological or pathological

The critical distinction is between a flexible flatfoot, in which the arch reconstitutes on tiptoe or with the Jack toe-raise test, and a rigid flatfoot, which does not correct and suggests tarsal coalition or arthritis
Flexible flatfoot is common and often asymptomatic in children, in whom it typically improves with growth and needs no active treatment when painless
In adults the leading cause of a progressive, painful, unilateral flatfoot is tibialis posterior tendon dysfunction

The too-many-toes sign, in which more lateral toes are visible from behind because of forefoot abduction, and an inability to perform a single-limb heel raise both point to tibialis posterior insufficiency
Examination should test arch flexibility, hindfoot correction on heel raise, gastrocnemius tightness, and the integrity and power of the tibialis posterior tendon
Weight-bearing radiographs assess alignment and arthritis, while ultrasound or MRI evaluates the tibialis posterior tendon and MRI or CT identifies a tarsal coalition

Management ranges from orthoses, medial arch support, physiotherapy with tibialis posterior strengthening, and calf stretching to tendon reconstruction, osteotomy, or arthrodesis in advanced deformity
reference.pathophysiology: Pes planus reflects failure of the structures that maintain the medial longitudinal arch, which depends on the bony architecture, the spring and plantar ligaments and plantar fascia, and dynamic support from the tibialis posterior. In flexible flatfoot the arch collapses on standing but reconstitutes when load is removed or the great toe is dorsiflexed, tightening the windlass mechanism of the plantar fascia. Adult acquired flatfoot most often develops when the tibialis posterior tendon degenerates and elongates, so that it can no longer invert and lock the hindfoot for an efficient heel raise; the hindfoot drifts into valgus, the forefoot abducts, and the medial arch progressively flattens, giving the too-many-toes appearance and a failed single-limb heel raise. If uncorrected the deformity becomes fixed and secondary arthritis develops. A rigid flatfoot instead reflects an underlying structural cause such as tarsal coalition, arthritis, or neuromuscular imbalance. A tight gastrocnemius commonly coexists and increases deforming forces on the midfoot.
additionalDifferentials: Tibialis posterior tendon dysfunction as the cause of acquired flatfoot
Tarsal coalition producing a rigid or peroneal-spastic flatfoot
Inflammatory arthropathy such as rheumatoid disease
Charcot neuroarthropathy in the diabetic or neuropathic foot
Accessory navicular contributing to medial arch symptoms
Neuromuscular flatfoot from cerebral palsy or other conditions
additionalInvestigations: Standing clinical examination with the tiptoe and single-limb heel-raise tests to assess flexibility and hindfoot correction
Assessment of tibialis posterior power and tenderness and of gastrocnemius tightness with the Silfverskiold test
Weight-bearing foot and ankle radiographs to measure alignment and detect arthritis
Ultrasound or MRI of the tibialis posterior tendon where dysfunction is suspected
CT or MRI to identify and characterise a tarsal coalition in a rigid flatfoot
Pedobarography to map abnormal plantar loading where relevant
Inflammatory markers and serology if inflammatory arthritis is suspected
redFlags: A rigid, painful flatfoot that does not correct on tiptoe, suggesting tarsal coalition, arthritis, or Charcot change
Rapidly progressive unilateral adult flatfoot with medial pain indicating tibialis posterior rupture
A hot, swollen, deformed foot in a neuropathic or diabetic patient suggesting Charcot neuroarthropathy
Features of inflammatory arthritis with symmetrical joint involvement
Neurological signs suggesting a neuromuscular cause of the deformity
reference.prognosis: Physiological flexible flatfoot in children usually improves with growth and rarely causes long-term problems. Adult acquired flatfoot from tibialis posterior dysfunction is progressive if untreated, moving from a flexible, correctable deformity to a fixed one with arthritis; early orthotic and physiotherapy treatment can control symptoms, and staged reconstructive surgery can restore alignment, whereas established rigid deformity may ultimately require arthrodesis.
pitfalls: Over-treating an asymptomatic flexible paediatric flatfoot that would resolve with growth
Failing to distinguish flexible from rigid deformity and missing a tarsal coalition
Overlooking tibialis posterior dysfunction as the cause of a painful adult flatfoot until it becomes fixed
Missing a tight gastrocnemius that must be addressed for correction to succeed
Not recognising Charcot neuroarthropathy in the diabetic foot presenting as a collapsing arch
references: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle
management: Reassurance and observation for asymptomatic flexible flatfoot in children, which typically improves with growth
Supportive footwear, medial arch orthoses, gastrocnemius stretching and physiotherapy for symptomatic flexible flatfoot
For adult acquired flatfoot from tibialis posterior dysfunction, use bracing or immobilisation and early tibialis posterior strengthening, with weight reduction
Surgical reconstruction for progressive or refractory flexible deformity, combining tendon transfer with a medialising calcaneal osteotomy
Arthrodesis for a rigid or arthritic flatfoot, and resection or fusion for a symptomatic tarsal coalition
Orthopaedic and podiatry follow-up to monitor progression from a flexible to a fixed deformity
